name: Tui tui tui (退！退！退！)
blurb: A "Back off!" chant from a viral 2022 Douyin clip, now used to ward off bad luck
title: Tui Tui Tui (退退退) Meme: Meaning and Origin
description: "退！退！退！" (tui tui tui, "back off!") comes from a 2022 street-argument video that went viral on Douyin. Now it is a joking chant to ward off anything unwanted.
h1: What is the "tui tui tui" (退退退) meme?
answer: "退！退！退！" (tuì tuì tuì, "back! back! back!" or "begone!") comes from a street-argument video: a woman running a roadside stall, confronted by a driver over the space she was using, stamps her feet and lunges forward with fencing-like jabs while shouting "退！退！退！". The clip went viral on Douyin in late May 2022, and comment sections filled with the phrase and fencing emoji. Today it means "go away" and is put after anything unwanted, as in 霉运退退退 (bad luck, begone).

body: The original clip was filmed by a passer-by. The woman's foot-stamping rhythm and lunging gestures look like she is casting a banishing spell, and that absurdity turned it into stickers and imitation videos. News commentary at the time noted that the exact cause of the argument was never verified.
In everyday use the phrase has nothing to do with the original dispute. It simply means "back off" or "stay away", said in an exaggerated, playful way rather than in real anger.

Event
rows: The street-argument clip spreads on Douyin and the "退！退！退！" chant is reposted everywhere
退退退 trends, and comment sections fill with the phrase plus fencing emoji

"X退退退" becomes an all-purpose formula for warding off bad luck, illness or bad weather

ul: Before exams: "挂科退！退！退！" (Failing grades, begone!)
Against bad luck: "水逆退退退，好运快来。" (Mercury retrograde, back off; good luck, come in.)
Watching a drama: "这个反派退退退。" (Villain, get out of here.)
Refusing overtime: "周末加班退退退。" (Weekend overtime, begone.)

body: Tui tui tui peaked in 2022 and is now a familiar older meme. The formula is so handy that it still shows up in comments and good-luck wishes, especially around exams, illness and bad streaks. Aim it at situations, not at real people, and leave the people in the original clip alone.

faq.q: Where does "tui tui tui" come from?
faq.a: From a passer-by's video of a street argument in which a woman running a stall stamps her feet and makes fencing-like jabs while shouting "退！退！退！". It went viral on Douyin in May 2022.

faq.q: Why do people post fencing emoji with it?
faq.a: The fencing emoji copy her lunging, sword-like gestures. A row of fencing emoji plus 退退退 became the standard comment format.
Put it after anything unwanted to mean "go away", such as 霉运退退退 (bad luck, begone) or 感冒退退退 (cold, go away), half joke and half good-luck charm.
